To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the capacity to govern urban flood risk is influenced by the probability and impact of floods, national imposed institutional settings, and the authority to secure long term financial support.
“Contextual factors influence capacity-priorities and may enable learning between cities”.

(i) crosscutting contextual conditions may explain differences in priorities of governance capacity development to address flood risk, and (ii) three contextual factors, namely flood probability and impact, national imposed institutional setting, and the level of authority to obtain long-term financial support, are identified that may influence capacity-building priorities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how contextual factors influence capacity-development in urban flood governance.
the role of contextual differences in explaining capacity-building priorities in the governance of urban flood risk.
understanding the role of contextual conditions in the capacity to govern urban flood risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the three crosscutting contextual conditions are important to consider when developing governance capacity to address flood risk.

the three identified contextual factor may explain differences in the priorities to develop governance capacity in the four case cities, and the framework of nine conditions with 27 indicators may facilitate a better understanding and learning about governance capacity in cities.
cities with a high level of authority to raise funds and with a high probability and impact of floods should focus on developing capacity to reduce the impact of floods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more flood risk a city is confronted with and the more authority a city has to develop capacity, the more capacity is needed.
context matters and should be taken into account when developing capacity for flood risk management in cities.
the context in which a city is located is of critical importance for the development of governance capacity to reduce urban flood risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the role of context should be taken into consideration when assessing governance capacity and that a more comprehensive understanding of governance capacity may be achieved through cross-case comparison.
cities can learn from each other by comparing their capacity-development priorities.
cities should consider the contextual factors when assessing capacity to govern urban flood risk.
